questions.title: Why does the token-level importance ratio in GRPO fail as a valid importance sampling weight?
questions.question_body: In the GSPO paper, the authors argue that GRPO's token-level importance ratio $w_{i,t}(\theta) = \frac{\pi_\theta(y_{i,t} | x, y_{i,<t})}{\pi_{\theta_\text{old}}(y_{i,t} | x, y_{i,<t})}$ is a misapplication of importance sampling. They state that because this weight is based on a single sample $y_{i,t}$ from each next-token distribution, it "fails to perform the intended distribution-correction role." However, importance sampling can technically be applied with any number of samples, including $N=1$. So what exactly makes the token-level ratio invalid? Is the issue that the expectation being estimated is over sequences, not tokens? Or is it about variance accumulation across the token-level ratios within a sequence? I would appreciate a more precise explanation of why the single-sample argument invalidates the token-level importance weight.

questions.title: Why is the length-normalized geometric mean used for the sequence-level importance ratio in GSPO?
questions.question_body: GSPO defines the sequence-level importance ratio as $s_i(\theta) = \left( \frac{\pi_\theta(y_i | x)}{\pi_{\theta_\text{old}}(y_i | x)} \right)^{\frac{1}{|y_i|}} = \exp\left( \frac{1}{|y_i|} \sum_{t=1}^{|y_i|} \log \frac{\pi_\theta(y_{i,t} | x, y_{i,<t})}{\pi_{\theta_\text{old}}(y_{i,t} | x, y_{i,<t})} \right)$. The paper says length normalization is adopted to "reduce the variance and to control $s_i(\theta)$ within a unified numerical range." But why is the geometric mean (i.e., the $1/|y_i|$ exponent) the right choice here? Wouldn't the raw sequence-level ratio $\frac{\pi_\theta(y_i | x)}{\pi_{\theta_\text{old}}(y_i | x)}$ be the theoretically correct importance weight for sequence-level importance sampling? Does using the geometric mean break the theoretical guarantees of importance sampling, or is it still a valid importance weight in some sense?

questions.title: How does GSPO weight all tokens equally in the gradient while GRPO does not?
questions.question_body: The paper's gradient analysis (Section 3.2) claims that the key distinction between GSPO and GRPO is how they weight the gradients of log likelihoods of tokens. The GSPO gradient is $\sum_{t} s_i(\theta) \widehat{A}_i \cdot \frac{1}{|y_i|} \nabla_\theta \log \pi_\theta(y_{i,t}|x,y_{i,<t})$, while the GRPO gradient is $\sum_t \widehat{A}_i \cdot \frac{1}{|y_i|} w_{i,t}(\theta) \nabla_\theta \log \pi_\theta(y_{i,t}|x,y_{i,<t})$. The paper says GSPO weights all tokens equally because $s_i(\theta)$ is shared across all tokens, whereas GRPO uses per-token weights $w_{i,t}(\theta)$. But in GSPO, doesn't $s_i(\theta)$ still multiply each token's gradient? So isn't the weighting still uneven in some sense—it's just that the weight is the same for all tokens? Is the claim simply that a uniform weight across tokens is more stable than per-token varying weights?

questions.title: Why does the GSPO-token variant use stop-gradient, and how does it preserve the sequence-level importance ratio?
questions.question_body: The GSPO-token variant defines $s_{i,t}(\theta) = \mathrm{sg}[s_i(\theta)] \cdot \frac{\pi_\theta(y_{i,t}|x,y_{i,<t})}{\mathrm{sg}[\pi_\theta(y_{i,t}|x,y_{i,<t})]}$, where $\mathrm{sg}$ stops the gradient. The paper says this is numerically equal to $s_i(\theta)$ since the second fraction equals 1. But in the gradient derivation, the $s_i(\theta)$ factor reappears without stop-gradient. I'm confused: if $s_i(\theta)$ is detached in the forward pass, how does its gradient flow through in the backward pass? Is the stop-gradient only on the token-level ratio part, while the sequence-level $s_i(\theta)$ retains its gradient? What is the purpose of this construction versus directly using $s_i(\theta) \cdot \widehat{A}_{i,t}$?

questions.title: Why does GSPO clip far more tokens than GRPO but still achieve better training efficiency?
questions.question_body: The paper reports a counter-intuitive finding: GSPO clips two orders of magnitude more tokens than GRPO (Figure 2), yet achieves higher training efficiency. The authors interpret this as evidence that GRPO's token-level gradient estimates are "inherently noisy and inefficient." But if GSPO is discarding so many more samples from gradient estimation, shouldn't it have less data to learn from? Is the argument that the clipped samples in GSPO are genuinely harmful (off-policy), so removing them is beneficial, while in GRPO the per-token clipping doesn't effectively remove harmful samples? Also, how can clipping at the sequence level remove more tokens than clipping at the token level—shouldn't token-level clipping be more fine-grained and thus clip fewer tokens?

questions.title: How does GSPO resolve the expert-activation volatility problem in MoE models without Routing Replay?
questions.question_body: The paper explains that in MoE models, after a gradient update, roughly 10% of experts activated for the same response change between $\pi_\theta$ and $\pi_{\theta_\text{old}}$, causing token-level importance ratios $w_{i,t}(\theta)$ to fluctuate drastically. The previous solution (Routing Replay) cached and reused old routing modes. The paper claims GSPO avoids this because it "focuses only on the sequence likelihood and is not sensitive to the individual token likelihood." But $s_i(\theta)$ is computed from token-level likelihoods (via the geometric mean of token ratios). If the experts change for some tokens, won't those token likelihoods change, affecting $s_i(\theta)$? Is the argument that the averaging in $s_i(\theta)$ smooths out the fluctuations from the ~10% of affected tokens?

questions.title: Why are the clipping ranges in GSPO (3e-4, 4e-4) so much smaller than in GRPO (0.2, 0.27)?
questions.question_body: The paper mentions that GSPO uses clipping ranges of $[1-3\times10^{-4}, 1+4\times10^{-4}]$ while GRPO uses $[0.8, 1.27]$. The paper briefly notes that "the clipping ranges in GSPO and in previous algorithms typically differ in order of magnitude due to the distinct definitions of importance ratios." But this is a huge difference—GRPO allows the ratio to deviate by ~20-27% while GSPO allows only ~0.03-0.04%. Why is such a tiny clipping range sufficient for GSPO? Is it because $s_i(\theta)$, being a geometric mean of token ratios, naturally has much lower variance than individual token ratios $w_{i,t}(\theta)$? And are the asymmetric clipping ranges (different left and right bounds) motivated by something specific?

questions.title: What does "model collapse" mean in the context of GRPO training, and why is it irreversible?
questions.question_body: The paper repeatedly mentions that GRPO can lead to "catastrophic and irreversible model collapse" during RL training of large language models. The authors state that once collapse occurs, resuming training is unavailing even when reverting to a previous checkpoint, tuning hyperparameters, extending generation length, or switching queries. What exactly constitutes "model collapse" here—is it the model generating degenerate/repetitive outputs, losing its reasoning ability, or something else? And what makes it irreversible? If you revert to a previous checkpoint, shouldn't you be able to resume from a known-good state? Is the irreversibility due to the optimizer state (e.g., momentum in Adam) being corrupted, or is there something deeper going on?

questions.title: How does GSPO's sequence-level approach help with precision discrepancies between training and inference engines?
questions.question_body: In Section 5.4, the paper claims that GSPO can directly use likelihoods from the inference engine (e.g., SGLang, vLLM) without recomputing them in the training engine (e.g., Megatron), because sequence-level likelihoods are "more tolerant of precision discrepancies." Why would a sequence-level likelihood $\pi_\theta(y|x) = \prod_t \pi_\theta(y_t|x,y_{<t})$ be more robust to floating-point precision differences than individual token likelihoods? Since the sequence likelihood is a product of token likelihoods, wouldn't precision errors compound? Or is the argument that the geometric mean in $s_i(\theta)$ averages out the precision noise? What specific precision discrepancies exist between training and inference engines that cause problems at the token level but not the sequence level?

questions.title: Is GSPO's sequence-level importance ratio still a valid importance sampling estimator?
questions.question_body: The paper motivates GSPO by arguing that the importance sampling weight should match the unit of reward (sequence level). The standard importance sampling estimator for a sequence-level expectation would use the ratio $\frac{\pi_\theta(y|x)}{\pi_{\theta_\text{old}}(y|x)}$. However, GSPO uses the length-normalized version $s_i(\theta) = \left(\frac{\pi_\theta(y|x)}{\pi_{\theta_\text{old}}(y|x)}\right)^{1/|y|}$. Does this modified ratio still yield an unbiased estimator of the sequence-level expectation? It seems like the normalization changes the expected value of the estimator. Is GSPO sacrificing unbiasedness for lower variance, similar to how PPO's clipping sacrifices unbiasedness for stability? The paper doesn't explicitly discuss whether GSPO's estimator is unbiased.
